explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:1 says the man "went to reside in the land of Moab." That is the land east of the Dead Sea. A famine emptied the shelves in Judah, so Elimelech packed up the family and moved to where there was food.
Not Egypt, baker. Ruth 1:1 names "the land of Moab" as the place they went to reside. Egypt is not in this verse. The family went east across the Jordan to Moab, not south to Egypt.
The text says "the land of Moab" (Ruth 1:1), not Edom. Edom is a different land to the south. Moab was the destination because that is where they could find food during the famine.
Ruth 1:4 says the two wives were "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." Ruth is the Moabitess who will stick with Naomi all the way to Bethlehem. That is the name the verse gives.
Not Rachel, friend. Ruth 1:4 gives the names: "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." Rachel is Jacob's wife from Genesis. Here the second daughter-in-law is Ruth the Moabitess.
The verse says "the other named Ruth" (Ruth 1:4). Dinah is Jacob's daughter in Genesis. In this story, the two Moabite women are Orpah and Ruth, so Ruth is the name you are looking for.

Ruth 1:5 says "both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband." Ten years in Moab and she loses both boys. She was left alone with no husband and no sons.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: That is not what happened. Ruth 1:5 says "both Mahlon and Chilion also died." The house did not burn; the sons died. Naomi was left "without her two sons and without her husband."

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: No sickness here, baker. Ruth 1:5 tells us "both Mahlon and Chilion also died." It was death that took them, and Naomi was the one left grieving, not sick herself.

Ruth 1:6 says Naomi heard "that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food." The famine was over in Judah and the LORD had provided food. That is the news that gets Naomi moving back home.
Not a king. Ruth 1:6 says the LORD "had attended to His people by providing them with food." It was food, not a new ruler. The famine had ended.
The text says "providing them with food" (Ruth 1:6), not victory in battle. Naomi heard the LORD had given His people food, so she prepared to leave Moab.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:8 records Naomi saying, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home." She sends them back to their own families in Moab and blesses them for their kindness to her and to her dead.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: She does not tell them to hurry. Ruth 1:8 has her saying, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home." Naomi is sending them home to their mothers, not urging them to walk faster.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: Actually, she tells them to go back. Ruth 1:8 says, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home." She does not ask them to stay with her on the road to Judah.
That is right. Ruth 1:9 says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." Naomi is wishing them remarriage and a home of their own in Moab. True.
No, it is true. Ruth 1:9 says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." Naomi's blessing talks about each of them finding rest in a new husband's home.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:10 says they wept aloud and said, "Surely we will return with you to your people." Both daughters-in-law want to go with Naomi to Judah. That is the line that starts the whole conversation.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: They said the opposite. Ruth 1:10 records them saying, "Surely we will return with you to your people." They wanted to go with her, not stay behind in Moab.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Not just a visit. Ruth 1:10 says, "Surely we will return with you to your people." They planned to travel with Naomi all the way to Bethlehem, not promise a future visit.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:13 has Naomi asking if they would wait: "...would you wait for them to grow up?" She points out that even if she had sons, the girls would have to wait years for them to grow.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: That is not her question. Ruth 1:13 asks "...would you wait for them to grow up?" She talks about waiting for sons to mature, not about raising them as their own.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Not that one. Ruth 1:13 records her asking "...would you wait for them to grow up?" It is about waiting years for sons, not going ahead to Bethlehem.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:13 says "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." Naomi says it is much more bitter for her because the LORD Himself has acted against her. That is the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Not the people of Judah. Ruth 1:13 says "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She points to the LORD, not to any group of people, as the source of her bitterness.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text does not say that. Ruth 1:13 has Naomi saying "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She blames the LORD's hand, not the Moabites or anyone else.
Yes, that is true. Ruth 1:14 says "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye." The verse shows Orpah saying farewell with a kiss before she heads back to her own people.
No, it is true. Ruth 1:14 says "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye." That is exactly what the text says happened before Orpah left.
No, Ruth did not go back. Ruth 1:14 says "Ruth clung to her." While Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, Ruth stayed right there with Naomi. So the statement is false.
Right, that is false. Ruth 1:14 says "Ruth clung to her." Ruth did not go back with Orpah; she held on to Naomi and went with her to Bethlehem.
That is true. Ruth 1:15 records Naomi saying, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home." Naomi urges Ruth to do the same as Orpah.
It is true, baker. Ruth 1:15 says Naomi told Ruth to "follow her back home." Naomi wanted Ruth to go back with Orpah to Moab.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:16 says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." Ruth adopts not just Naomi's family but also Naomi's God, the LORD. That is the promise.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Not that one. Ruth 1:16 says "your God will be my God," not anything about housework. She promises to share Naomi's people and Naomi's LORD.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:16 says "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." She does not mention learning customs; she promises to share Naomi's God and people.
Ruth 1:17 says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." Ruth swears that only death will part them. She is all in.
Not distance. Ruth 1:17 says "if anything but death separates you and me." She does not say distance; she says death is the only thing that will separate them.
Ruth 1:17 says "anything but death." Marriage is not mentioned as the separator; death is. Ruth is saying nothing but death will keep her from Naomi.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:18 says when Naomi saw Ruth was determined, "she stopped trying to persuade her." Naomi sees the resolve and gives up the argument. They travel together to Bethlehem.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: No, she stops persuading. Ruth 1:18 says Naomi "stopped trying to persuade her" when she saw Ruth was determined. She did not send her back after Orpah.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: Not that. Ruth 1:18 says Naomi stopped trying to persuade Ruth. She did not tell her to wait in Moab; she accepted that Ruth was coming with her.
Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?" They recognize her but are shocked to see her back after all those years. That is their reaction.
Not that question. Ruth 1:19 records the women saying, "Can this be Naomi?" They do not ask about her husband first; they just cannot believe it is her.
They knew who she was. Ruth 1:19 says they exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?" They recognized her, but the whole town was stirred by her return.

Ruth 1:20 says Naomi told them, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." Mara means bitter, and that is the name she wants now. Naomi is the old name; Mara is how she feels.
Not Hannah. Ruth 1:20 says, "Call me Mara." Hannah is a different woman from 1 Samuel. Here Naomi asks to be called Mara because of her bitterness.
The text says Mara. Ruth 1:20 records Naomi saying, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." Leah is Jacob's wife from Genesis; here it is Mara.
No, that is false. Ruth 1:21 says the opposite: "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." Naomi went away full and came back empty, not the other way around.
That is right, it is false. Ruth 1:21 says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." The text says she left full and returned empty, so the statement is false.
Ruth 1:22 says they arrived "at the beginning of the barley harvest." Barley is the first grain to come in, so it is early spring. That is the season the text names.
Not wheat. Ruth 1:22 says "the beginning of the barley harvest." Wheat comes later in the season; barley is the early crop.
Not olive. Ruth 1:22 specifies "the barley harvest." Olives are harvested later in the year, but the text names barley.
